# The April Third Movement {#sec-4-07}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1965–1971
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What happens when the people inside the machine can see it?

**The answer.** The machine changes its legal address. Stanford's students spent
four years documenting the university's military research and demanding the
university take responsibility for it. They won the argument and lost the object:
the Faculty Senate banned classified research on campus, and the trustees sold
the Stanford Research Institute to itself. The research continued. What ended was
the university's obligation to answer for it.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control, defended by restructuring. This is the
chapter that shows what the mechanism does under pressure, which is the only way
to demonstrate that it is a mechanism and not a mood. Confronted with a demand for
accountability, the institution did not reform and did not refuse. It
reorganised — the same move the Big Four made with the Contract and Finance
Company, and the same move Act IV will show platforms making with contractor
workforces and offshore subsidiaries.

**The key fact.** The protesters' central demand was that Stanford exercise
*more* control over SRI. The trustees' answer was to give SRI away. On 16 May
1969 police used tear gas on students who were protesting the divestment,
because separation was never what they had asked for.

**The human anchor.** The occupiers themselves, and specifically what they did
with the building. During nine days inside the Applied Electronics Laboratory
they ran a child care centre in one lab, a bookstore in another, rooms named for
Eldridge Cleaver and Che Guevara in two more, and turned the laboratory printshop
into an underground press. They published the classified research they found.
They titled it *The Goods on AEL*.

**Excluded voices.** Inverted here, and the chapter should be honest about the
inversion. These are not the powerless; they are the children of the elite,
objecting from inside. The people actually on the receiving end of
counterinsurgency research were in Vietnam and had no vote in Dinkelspiel
Auditorium. Say so. The chapter is stronger for conceding that the conscience of
the machine is still the machine.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the mechanism survives exposure by showing
that its most effective internal challenge produced a change of corporate
structure rather than a change of activity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

At 10:45 on the morning of 9 April 1969, about four hundred Stanford students
walked into the Applied Electronics Laboratory and shut it down. Roughly two
million dollars of classified Defense Department research was under way inside.
They stayed nine days.

The chapter builds to that and then past it, because the occupation is not the
story. The story is what the university did in response.

It starts in 1965, when it becomes known on campus that SRI — the research
institute Stanford had founded in 1946 and still owned — holds two contracts
concerning chemical warfare. Concern hardens in 1967 when students learn SRI has
taken contracts related to Southeast Asia, and picketing begins outside its
Menlo Park buildings. The numbers matter and the chapter gives them carefully:
across 1950–65, only nineteen of five hundred and eighty-two doctoral and
engineering theses in electrical engineering were classified. By 1968, close to
thirty-five percent of the department's electronics research funding was
classified work. Something had changed, and the students could read it in the
budget.

On 3 April 1969 roughly seven hundred people fill Dinkelspiel Auditorium and the
scattered factions reorganise into one coalition, which takes its name from the
date. Their demands are specific: stricter trustee guidelines for SRI; an end to
all classified research at the university and at SRI; an end to all chemical and
biological warfare work and all counterinsurgency work at both institutions,
classified or not; and a public trustees' meeting on the question. Six days later
they take the building.

They win, quickly and on paper. The engineering dean announces his school will
accept no further classified contracts and will wind down existing ones. On 24
April the academic senate passes guidelines that effectively banish classified
research from campus. The occupiers leave the AEL on 18 April under threat of
suspension.

Then the trustees answer the SRI question, and the answer is the chapter's
argument. A joint committee had already recommended, nine votes to twelve
members, that Stanford sell the institute — book value twenty-five million,
estimated worth forty-five. In January 1970 the trustees set the terms: SRI would
be sold to itself, paying one percent of gross operating revenues against a
twenty-five million dollar price. The chemical warfare work, the counterinsurgency
work, the classified contracts — none of it stopped. It simply stopped being
Stanford's.

The chapter's coda is the tear gas. On 16 May 1969, students blocking traffic
near the SRI building were dispersed by police after four hours. They were
protesting the divestment. They had asked the university to take responsibility;
it had taken its name off the door instead.

And the research followed the money out. Researchers left the AEL for SRI, taking
eight hundred thousand dollars in contracts with them. The chokepoint had not been
closed. It had been moved four miles, to a building nobody could hold a sit-in
about, because it no longer belonged to anyone the students could petition.
:::

## Beats

1. **Hook.** 10:45 a.m., 9 April 1969. Four hundred students, one building, two
   million dollars of classified work stopped by people walking through a door.
2. **Rewind to 1965.** Two chemical warfare contracts become known. What SRI was
   and why Stanford owned it — connect back to ch. 4 on the defence corridor.
3. **1967.** Southeast Asia contracts. Picketing at Menlo Park.
4. **The budget as evidence.** Nineteen of five hundred and eighty-two theses
   classified, 1950–65, against thirty-five percent of electronics research
   funding classified by 1968. The students were reading a real change.
5. **3 April 1969.** Dinkelspiel, seven hundred people, the coalition forms and
   names itself for the day. List the four demands precisely — the first one is
   *more* university control, which is the chapter's hinge.
6. **The occupation.** Nine days. The child care centre, the bookstore, the rooms
   named for Cleaver and Guevara, the printshop turned press. *The Goods on AEL*
   and *Declassified*. Students publishing the classified research they found.
7. **The concessions.** The engineering dean's announcement. The academic senate's
   24 April guidelines. Departure from the building on 18 April.
8. **The restructuring.** The joint committee's recommendation to sell. January
   1970 terms: SRI sold to itself, one percent of gross revenues up to twenty-five
   million.
9. **The tear gas, 16 May 1969.** Students protesting the divestment. Make the
   irony land without editorialising; the facts carry it.
10. **The follow-the-money detail.** Researchers leaving AEL for SRI with eight
    hundred thousand dollars in contracts.
11. **The concession about the protesters.** They were inside the elite, arguing
    from within it. The people subject to the research had no representation in
    that room.
12. **Landing.** Naming the move: pressure produced reorganisation, not reform.
    Point back to the Contract and Finance Company in Act I and forward to Act
    V's contractor workforces. Same manoeuvre, three centuries of costume.

**Source note.** SRI's own institutional history characterises the students'
demands as "usually unfounded" and its chemical warfare work as "almost
exclusively defensive." That is an interested party describing itself. Cite it as
SRI's position, not as the record.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What happens when the people inside the machine can see it?
:::

At a quarter to eleven on the morning of 9 April 1969, about four hundred
Stanford students walked into the Applied Electronics Laboratory and stopped
work.

Roughly two million dollars of classified Defense Department research was under
way in the building. The students stayed nine days.

They won the argument almost immediately. Within two weeks the faculty senate
had effectively banned classified research on campus. And the university's
answer to their central demand was to give away the thing they had asked it to
take responsibility for, which is the subject of this chapter.

## What they had been reading

The movement did not begin in 1969 and it did not begin with slogans. It began
with people reading contracts.

Concern surfaced in 1965, when it became known on campus that the Stanford-owned
Research Institute in Menlo Park held two contracts concerning chemical warfare.
It intensified in 1967 when students learned that SRI had taken on work related
to Southeast Asia, and picketing began outside the Menlo Park buildings that
April.

The numbers they assembled were the strongest part of their case. Across the
fifteen years from 1950 to 1965, only nineteen of five hundred and eighty-two
doctoral and engineering theses in Stanford's electrical engineering department
had been classified, more than half of those during the Korean War. By 1968,
close to thirty-five per cent of the department's electronics research funding
was classified work, concentrated in the Applied Electronics Laboratory.

Something had changed, and it was legible in the budget. The students were not
imagining a transformation of their university; they had documented one.

## 3 April

On 3 April 1969 roughly seven hundred people met in Dinkelspiel Auditorium and
the several existing factions — the campus chapter of Students for a Democratic
Society, an SRI coalition, and others — reorganised into a single body that took
its name from the date.

Their demands were four, and the first is the hinge of this chapter.

They wanted the trustees to impose stricter guidelines on SRI. They wanted an
end to all classified research at the university and at SRI. They wanted an end
to all chemical and biological warfare work and all counterinsurgency work at
both institutions, whether classified or not. And they wanted a public meeting
of the full board of trustees on the question.

Read the first demand again. They were asking the university to exercise more
control over its research institute, not less. They wanted the institution to
own what it owned.

## Nine days

Six days later they took the building, and what they did inside it is the most
revealing thing in the chapter.

They ran a child care centre in one laboratory. They set up a bookstore in
another, and named two rooms for Eldridge Cleaver and Che Guevara. A high school
auxiliary operated in the basement. They held continuous open meetings and voted
on everything.

And they used the laboratory's own printshop as a press. They went through the
material they found, and published it: a booklet called *The Goods on AEL*, and
a newsletter called *Declassified* that ran throughout the occupation.

Students in a building they had occupied, printing the classified research they
found there, on the equipment they found there. It is the clearest available
illustration of the argument from Act II chapter 11 — that classification is
what makes the arrangement unaccountable — made by people who had simply removed
the classification.

The administration did not call the police into the AEL. President Kenneth
Pitzer, who had arrived the previous year, sought an outcome that avoided the
scenes at Columbia and Berkeley. Armed with emergency authority, he eventually
threatened suspension, and the students left on 18 April. He then closed the
laboratory to everybody, including its own staff, for a week.

## Winning on paper

The concessions came quickly.

Joseph Pettit, the dean of engineering, announced that the school would accept
no further classified contracts and would wind down the ones it held. On 24
April the academic senate adopted guidelines that effectively banished
classified research from the campus.

That is a comprehensive victory on the terms the movement had stated. Classified
research at Stanford essentially ended, and it has not returned in the form it
took in 1968.

## The restructuring

Then the trustees answered the SRI question, and the answer is why this chapter
exists.

A joint study committee of students, faculty, and administrators had been
appointed to consider the relationship. In April 1969 nine of its twelve members
recommended that Stanford sell the institute. SRI's book value was around
twenty-five million dollars and its actual worth was estimated at something
closer to forty-five. Some committee members wanted restrictive covenants
attached to any sale, prohibiting chemical weapons and counterinsurgency work. A
minority argued for the opposite course: that Stanford should take control and
redirect the institute, because divesting it would not address the substance at
all.

In January 1970 the trustees set the terms. SRI would be sold to itself, paying
one per cent of its gross operating revenues — which had been fifty-eight
million dollars in 1969 — up to a total of twenty-five million.

The chemical warfare work did not stop. The counterinsurgency work did not stop.
The classified contracts did not stop. What stopped was Stanford's ownership of
the institution doing them, and therefore any obligation to answer for it.

The research also followed the money out of the university. Researchers left the
Applied Electronics Laboratory for SRI, taking some eight hundred thousand
dollars in contracts and three hundred thousand in overhead with them, and SRI
closed its annex in the industrial park, which removed a target.

## The tear gas

On 16 May 1969 police used tear gas to disperse students blocking traffic near
the SRI building. They dispersed after about four hours.

They were protesting the divestment.

That sentence is the chapter, and it should be allowed to stand with no
commentary. The students had asked the university to take responsibility for
what it owned. The trustees had responded by ceasing to own it. And the
students, who understood perfectly well what had happened, were tear-gassed
while objecting to a decision that was formally a concession to them.

## What the movement was, honestly

The chapter owes one concession, and making it strengthens the argument.

These were not the powerless. They were students at one of the most expensive
private universities in the United States, most of them from comfortable
backgrounds, many of them shielded from the draft by the deferment their
enrolment provided. They were the elite objecting from inside it, and several of
them went on to conventional careers in the institutions they were protesting.

The people actually on the receiving end of counterinsurgency research were in
Southeast Asia and had no representation in Dinkelspiel Auditorium. Nobody
consulted them, and the movement's success or failure made no difference to them
that anyone has been able to trace.

That is worth saying plainly, because a book arguing that institutions reproduce
an elite should not exempt the elite's conscience from the analysis. The
conscience of the machine is still the machine.

## The manoeuvre named

What the trustees performed in 1970 was not reform and was not refusal. It was
reorganisation: a change in the legal ownership of an activity, leaving the
activity untouched and removing the party that could be held responsible for it.

Act I chapter 9 described the Contract and Finance Company, which put the
railroad's profits inside an entity with no public obligations. Act I chapter
10 described the Southern Pacific reincorporating in Kentucky while the track
stayed in California. Act III chapter 6 described a shoe company owning no
factories. Act IV will describe platform workforces held at arm's length through
contractors and drivers classified as independent.

Every one of these is the same move. When pressure arrives at a boundary, redraw
the boundary.

The most effective internal challenge the Stanford mechanism ever faced produced
a change in corporate structure. That is the strongest evidence in this book
that what it is describing is a mechanism rather than a set of choices, because
a set of choices can be argued with, and this could not.
